value: negative phototaxis at 400 nm rose with irradiance, reaching 57.14 ± 7.14% at 600 µW cm-2 (Y-tube, adults)

conditions: 25 ± 2 °C and 70 ± 5% relative humidity (Methods; the Abstract gives 25 ± 1 °C); twenty-five pairs of adults per replicate (both sexes; the paper did not examine sex-specific responses), three independent runs per treatment, 1 h per treatment, age and feeding status not stated; 30 min dark adaptation; screening irradiances 100, 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1000 µW cm-2; the page does not say whether arm sides were swapped or randomised; light and dark arms had the same height and visual background and no light but the LED stimulus; ± is the SE of replicate-level percentages (n = 3 runs); in binomial GLMs with Wald tests, predator negative phototaxis was significantly affected by wavelength (p < 0.001) and the wavelength x irradiance interaction (p = 0.0141) but not by irradiance alone (p = 0.2822), and no pairwise test of 600 µW cm-2 against other irradiances is reported; at 440 nm negative phototaxis peaked numerically at 44.42 ± 6.02% at 200 µW cm-2; in the same Results paragraph negative phototaxis was concentrated at 400 and 440 nm, and under several longer-wavelength conditions the difference between positive and negative phototaxis was reduced or reversed; laboratory Y-tube only, the Discussion calls for field or greenhouse validation

value: free-moving workers acquired a conditioned proboscis-extension response (PER) to guava odour more strongly than to mango odour

conditions: the number of bees, groups and colonies is not stated in the article (page summary); workers were collected at a hive entrance; learning of an odour-reward association, so this shows odour detection and discrimination through a conditioned response, not a detection threshold; the Discussion reports, in fragments, an average conditioned-PER probability of 75% for guava and 40% for mango by the sixth trial; with an unscented reward PER responses were low on day 1, with a scented reward they increased (chi2 = 20.9994, df = 1, p < 0.0001), and reward type was not a significant factor on day 2 (Abstract and Results); on day 1 guava gave a larger increase in conditioned response than mango (chi2 = 5.6365, df = 1, p < 0.05), and bees switched to a new odour on day 2 learned guava (chi2 = 3.6954, p < 0.05) but not mango; the two odour sources are different tissues and the text does not say their intensity was matched, so the guava-mango difference may reflect stimulus strength or composition; each experiment used a fixed odour sequence (Table 1); t-tests with 8 to 12 degrees of freedom suggest about 9 to 13 bees per comparison (auditor inference); individual bee differences were significant and not explained by the fixed factors, and age and health were not controlled (authors, per page summary)
